title: How to Automate Team Notifications and Task Routing in Chatwork with Jinba
summary: Chatwork approvals stall because standard integrations post a message and stop. Jinba Flows add two-way task routing, status polling, and a single audit trail.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- Most Chatwork integrations are one-directional: they post a message and stop, with no task-status retrieval or unified audit trail. For regulated Japanese operations teams, that gap is a compliance risk.
- A message is informational, while a task has a trackable lifecycle; approvals should use` CHATWORK_CREATE_TASK` so completion can be queried and routed back into the workflow.
- Chatwork is Japan's #1 business chat tool for six consecutive years, with over 7.05 million users across 321,000 companies, but API limits (300 requests/5 min; 10/10 sec for task creation) and non-expiring tokens require controlled orchestration.
- [Jinba Flow](https://flow.jinba.io/) closes the loop with two-way Chatwork tools, webhooks/polling, secrets management, and centralized audit logging. Start by storing the Chatwork API token in secrets and mapping your first trigger-to-task flow.


In Japanese enterprise approval workflows, requests are submitted, messages are sent in Chatwork, and follow-up remains manual. Tasks land in the wrong inbox, responsibility for the next action is unclear, and the audit trail is limited to whatever is recorded.


The underlying problem is structural. Most Chatwork integrations are one-directional. They post a notification and stop. There is no mechanism to track whether a task was completed, no way to route updates back into the originating workflow, and no centralized record of what happened. For operations teams in regulated industries, this gap is a compliance risk.


Jinba closes that gap with a complete trigger-to-audit workflow that treats Chatwork as a fully integrated, two-way endpoint rather than a simple message destination.


## Why Standard Chatwork Integrations Fall Short


The limitation of generic automation platforms is structural.[Zapier's Chatwork integration](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/40859029656973-How-to-get-started-with-Chatwork-on-Zapier) exposes no triggers and no searches, only three actions: Create Room, Create Task, and Send Message. Nothing in Chatwork can initiate a Zap. Every automation built on this pattern is fire-and-forget: a message goes out, and what happens next is invisible to the workflow.


The governance problem is equally significant. Operations teams managing approvals across multiple tools end up with fragmented logs, each system maintaining its own access controls with no unified audit trail. Auditors require a clear chain of accountability for every action taken. Fragmented records across disconnected tools make that requirement difficult to meet.


Jinba addresses both problems. Its[ChatWork Advanced](https://carnot.mintlify.app/en/pages/tools/communication/chatwork_advanced) toolset provides five purpose-built tools that together form a complete loop:


- ` CHATWORK_SEND_MESSAGE`
- ` CHATWORK_GET_MESSAGES`
- ` CHATWORK_CREATE_TASK`
- ` CHATWORK_GET_TASKS`
- ` CHATWORK_UPDATE_TASK_STATUS`


Combined with[SOC 2 Type II compliance](https://jinba.io/) , Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), end-to-end encryption, and centralized audit logging, Jinba provides the governance layer that basic integrations do not offer.


## Prerequisites


Before building a Chatwork automation workflow in Jinba, two accounts are required: a Chatwork account (Free or Paid) and a Jinba account.


The Chatwork API token is generated at` chatwork.com/service/packages/chatwork/subpackages/api/token.php` . One critical detail from the[Chatwork API documentation](https://developer.chatwork.com/docs/endpoints) : the API token carries no expiry and grants full account access. It must never be stored in source code or committed to a repository.


Jinba handles this through a secrets store. The token is referenced in flow configuration as` {{secrets.CHATWORK_API_TOKEN}}` , which means the credential never appears in plaintext within the workflow definition itself.


## Step 1: Triggering the Jinba Flow


Because Chatwork exposes no native triggers on standard automation platforms, every workflow begins inside Jinba. Triggers can be drawn from connected systems: a new record in a CRM, a submitted form, a scheduled job, or any upstream event that Jinba supports.


The workflow does not wait for Chatwork to signal that something happened. Jinba initiates the flow based on business logic, then reaches into Chatwork to notify and assign work. The Jinba documentation illustrates this with a` sales_data` step whose output feeds directly into a Chatwork message body.


## Step 2: Sending Messages and Creating Tasks with ChatWork Advanced


The distinction between a message and a task matters operationally. A message is informational; it delivers context. A task has a lifecycle: it is created, assigned, completed or left open, and its status is queryable. Treating every notification as a message loses the ability to track outcomes. Using` CHATWORK_CREATE_TASK` instead creates a record with a status that Jinba can retrieve later.


The following YAML, drawn directly from the Jinba documentation, shows how to send a notification within a Jinba Flow:


steps:
- name: send_notification
tool: CHATWORK_SEND_MESSAGE
params:
api_token: "{{secrets.CHATWORK_API_TOKEN}}"
room_id: 123456789
body: |
\[To:all\]
New high-priority sales lead assigned.
Summary: {{steps.sales_data.result.summary}}
Please review and take action.


Each element serves a specific function. The` api_token` field references the secrets store rather than a hardcoded value. The` room_id` targets the specific Chatwork room. The` body` field uses template interpolation to pull dynamic content from a previous step in the flow, in this case a summary produced by the` sales_data` step.


To create an assigned task instead of a message, replace` CHATWORK_SEND_MESSAGE` with` CHATWORK_CREATE_TASK` and include the relevant assignee and deadline parameters. The task then exists as a discrete, trackable unit inside Chatwork.


## Step 3: Closing the Loop with Task Status Updates


Retrieving task status from Chatwork and routing it into Jinba is the point at which chatwork automation becomes useful for operations teams. Jinba supports two methods.


**Method A: Polling with** **` CHATWORK_GET_TASKS`**


A subsequent step in the Jinba Flow calls` CHATWORK_GET_TASKS` at a configured interval to retrieve the current status of tasks in a given room. When a task is marked complete in Chatwork, the polling step detects the change and routes the workflow forward, triggering the next action whether that is an escalation, a log entry, or a confirmation message to a different channel.


**Method B: Real-time updates with Chatwork Webhooks**


For lower latency,[Chatwork Webhooks](https://developer.chatwork.com/docs/webhook) send an HTTPS POST to a Jinba endpoint whenever a configured event occurs, such as` message_created` or` mention_to_me` . This removes the need to poll at intervals.


Webhook configuration carries several constraints that enterprise teams need to account for:


- A maximum of 5 webhooks per account
- The endpoint must return HTTP 200 within 10 seconds of receiving the request
- Failed webhook notifications are not retried
- An auto-disable guard will deactivate a webhook if its error rate exceeds a threshold, requiring manual re-enablement
- All webhook requests must be verified using HMAC-SHA256 signature verification


The 10-second response window is the critical operational constraint. Chatwork's own developer documentation recommends an asynchronous pattern: the receiving endpoint acknowledges the request immediately and hands processing off to a queue. Jinba's architecture supports this pattern, ensuring the response window is met even when downstream processing takes longer.


## Step 4: Centralized Audit Logging


Every action in a Jinba Flow, including every Chatwork notification sent, every task created, and every status update retrieved, is captured in a centralized audit log. The log records structured events in the format` \[AUDIT\] role-assignment-update` , with timestamps and actor identifiers, as shown on the Jinba platform.


This single governance layer makes compliance reviews tractable. The problem with fragmented integrations is that logs live in separate systems with separate access controls and no unified view. Auditors cannot reconstruct a chain of accountability from disconnected records. Jinba's audit trail provides the complete sequence: what was triggered, what was sent to Chatwork, what task was created, who completed it, and when, all in one place.


## Advanced Considerations for Enterprise-Scale Automation


### API Rate Limits


According to Zapier's Chatwork integration documentation, Chatwork's API enforces rate limits that high-volume workflows encounter. The global limit is 300 requests per 5 minutes. Message and task creation endpoints carry a tighter ceiling of 10 requests per 10 seconds. Enterprise operations teams running approval workflows across many rooms simultaneously need throttling and backoff logic built into the integration layer. Jinba's flow engine handles retry and pacing at the orchestration level, keeping individual steps within the permitted request rate.


### Token Hygiene and Secrets Management


The non-expiring nature of the Chatwork API token is the highest-priority security concern in any Chatwork automation setup. A token exposed in a configuration file or source repository grants permanent, full-account access with no automatic remediation. Jinba's secrets store is the correct pattern: the token is stored once, referenced as` {{secrets.CHATWORK_API_TOKEN}}` in every flow that requires it, and never appears in plaintext within a flow definition or log output.


### Private and Air-Gapped Deployments


Jinba supports on-premise and private cloud hosting, and integrates with private AI models including AWS Bedrock Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Azure OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo, and self-hosted Llama 3 70B. For regulated Japanese enterprises with data residency requirements or strict network controls, this means the entire automation stack, from flow execution to Chatwork API calls, can operate within a controlled boundary. No data needs to traverse a public SaaS layer.


## What to Configure Next


[Chatwork](https://www.moomoo.com/news/post/44935839/kubell-chatwork-has-been-the-number-one-business-chat-domestic) holds the number one position in business chat usage in Japan for six consecutive years, with over 7.05 million users across more than 321,000 companies. For most Japanese enterprise operations teams, it is already the primary coordination layer. It can function either as a passive notification board or as an active, auditable workflow endpoint.


Jinba's ChatWork Advanced toolset, Flows engine, RBAC controls, and centralized audit logging make the second option achievable without custom development. The full automation loop, from trigger through notification, task assignment, status retrieval, and audit record, is configurable through documented YAML steps and Jinba's integration layer.


Start by visiting the Jinba ChatWork Advanced documentation to review the five available tools and the example flows. Store the Chatwork API token immediately in Jinba's secrets store before it appears anywhere else. Then map the first workflow: identify the upstream trigger, the Chatwork room that should receive the notification, and whether the outcome requires a trackable task or an informational message. From there, the audit trail is captured automatically.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### How do I automate Chatwork approval workflows with an audit trail?


Use Jinba's Chatwork Advanced toolset, which provides a two-way loop: trigger a Jinba Flow, create a trackable Chatwork task, retrieve its status, and log every action in a centralized audit trail. Unlike one-directional integrations, Jinba treats Chatwork as an operational endpoint rather than just a notification channel.


### What is the difference between a Chatwork message and a Chatwork task in automation?


A Chatwork message is informational and has no lifecycle, while a task is a discrete, assignable unit with a status that can be queried and updated. For approvals and compliance workflows, use` CHATWORK_CREATE_TASK` instead of` CHATWORK_SEND_MESSAGE` so the outcome remains trackable.


### How can I get task status updates from Chatwork back into Jinba?


Organizations can either poll with` CHATWORK_GET_TASKS` at configured intervals or use Chatwork Webhooks for real-time HTTPS callbacks. Polling is simpler but adds latency; webhooks are faster but require handling Chatwork's 10-second response window, signature verification, and failover constraints.


### Why do standard Chatwork integrations fail compliance audits?


Most standard integrations are fire-and-forget: they post a notification and then lose visibility. With no triggers, no status retrieval, and fragmented logs across tools, auditors cannot reconstruct who acted and when. Jinba closes this gap with centralized audit logging and Role-Based Access Control.


### What are the Chatwork API rate limits I need to plan for?


Chatwork enforces a global limit of 300 requests per 5 minutes, with message and task creation limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds. High-volume enterprise workflows should use an orchestration layer such as Jinba to add pacing, retries, and backoff rather than calling the API directly.


### How should I store my Chatwork API token in an automated workflow?


Store the token in Jinba's secrets store and reference it as` {{secrets.CHATWORK_API_TOKEN}}` . Never hardcode it in YAML, source code, or logs, because the Chatwork API token does not expire and grants full account access.


### Can I use Chatwork Webhooks with Jinba for real-time approvals?


Yes. Jinba can receive webhook events such as` message_created` or` mention_to_me` . However, Chatwork limits each account to 5 webhooks, requires HTTP 200 within 10 seconds, does not retry failed deliveries, and may auto-disable webhooks after repeated errors, so configure HMAC-SHA256 verification and asynchronous processing.


### Does Jinba support on-premise or private cloud Chatwork automation?


Yes. Jinba supports on-premise and private cloud deployments, including private AI models such as AWS Bedrock Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Azure OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo, and self-hosted Llama 3 70B. This keeps Chatwork automation and data within a controlled boundary for Japanese enterprises with residency requirements.


### What should I configure first to start automating Chatwork approvals with Jinba?


Start by storing the Chatwork API token in Jinba's secrets store, then review the five ChatWork Advanced tools. Map the first flow: choose the upstream trigger, decide whether the outcome needs a trackable task or an informational message, and identify the Chatwork room that should receive it.
